To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a diverse range and number of bacteria are present on prosthetic joint surfaces removed from patients with aseptic loosened and infected prostheses.

a diverse range (28 phylotypes in all) of bacteria are found on the surface of hip replacement joints removed from patients who have had revision surgery because of either infection or mechanical failure.
a diverse microflora was found on prosthetic hip joints, with Lysobacter being the dominant genus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of bacteria on the surfaces of clinically infected and uninfected prosthetic hip joint removed during revision arthoplasties.
the identification of bacteria on the surfaces of prosthetic hip replacements removed during revision arthoplasties.
a new approach to the study of bacteria on the surfaces of prosthetic hip joint components, which may have a role in the pathogenesis of prosthetic joint infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of a biofilm on the surface of a prosthetic joint, whether infected or not, is a risk factor in the failure of a joint replacement, and the organisms found within the biofilm may be aetiological factors.
the presence of Lysobacter and Lysobacter-related phylotypes is not a reliable indicator of infection.
the presence of L. enzymogenes in the biofilm of aseptically loosened prosthetic joint implants is not associated with the development of a clinical infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a diverse microflora is present on the surface on both infected and non-infeceted prostheses.
molecular methods are able to identify a more diverse micro-organism population than traditional microbiological culture techniques.
molecular detection methods identified a greater range of bacteria than traditional culture methods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a diverse microflora is present in the biofilm, and this microflora is more diverse than previously thought.
the microbiology of the prosthetic joint infection is complex.
the majority of the bacteria found on the surface of the implants were not detected with culture methods.
